claims.text: Intermediate thermal aging in FCC/B2 eutectic HEAs produces a transient ductile-brittle-ductile transition.
The transient brittle state is driven by growth and percolation of ordered B2 local-chemical-order domains.
A continuous ordered B2 morphology is less ductile than a morphology containing nanoscale or discrete B2 regions.
The initial microstructure is an FCC matrix containing discrete, non-percolating B2 precipitates or LCO clusters.
The initial material has a high dislocation density inherited from prior processing.
Aging at approximately 500–700 °C permits LCO growth and phase-boundary coarsening.
Strain rates of 10^-4 to 10^-3 s^-1 are representative of quasi-static mechanical testing for these alloys.
Classical impurity-driven grain-boundary embrittlement is thermodynamically suppressed in the proposed aging-temperature regime.
During intermediate aging, LCOs grow and coalesce into a continuous B2 network.
A continuous B2 network impedes dislocation glide.
Impeded dislocation motion forces deformation to localize.
Deformation localization caused by the B2 network produces brittle fracture.
At higher aging temperatures, Ostwald ripening or loss of long-range order breaks the percolating B2 path.
After the B2 phase becomes isolated, dislocations can bypass or shear the ordered domains.
Breaking the B2 percolation path restores ductility.
Ductility should first be high, then fall sharply to near zero, and subsequently recover.
The brittle regime correlates with the maximum volume fraction and connectivity of the ordered phase.
The brittle regime does not correlate with grain-size reduction.
Classical grain-boundary embrittlement models predict monotonic property changes or embrittlement solely at low temperatures.

The hypothesis is falsified if brittleness begins while B2 domains remain below the connectivity percolation threshold, or if brittleness instead tracks grain-boundary segregation while B2 remains non-percolated.
